claim: Active flight requires the ability to efficiently fuel bursts of costly locomotion while maximizing energy conservation during non-flying times.
source: Active flight requires the ability to efficiently fuel bursts of costly locomotion while maximizing energy conservation during non-flying times.
evidence: This is a general statement about flight energetics that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum use a novel, cyclic, bradycardic state that reduces daily energetic expenditure by 10%.
source: Miniaturized heart rate telemetry shows that they use a novel, cyclic, bradycardic state that reduces daily energetic expenditure by 10% and counteracts heart rates as high as 900 bpm during flight.
evidence: This claim is supported by heart rate telemetry data collected from free-ranging bats and analyzed to calculate energy savings.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum have heart rates as high as 900 bpm during flight.
source: Miniaturized heart rate telemetry shows that they use a novel, cyclic, bradycardic state that reduces daily energetic expenditure by 10% and counteracts heart rates as high as 900 bpm during flight.
evidence: This is directly measured from heart rate telemetry data during flight.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum support flight with some of the fastest metabolic incorporation rates in vertebrates.
source: Uroderma bilobatum support flight with some of the fastest metabolic incorporation rates and dynamic circulating cortisol in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by stable isotope diet switching experiments measuring δ13C in exhaled CO2.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum have dynamic circulating cortisol in vertebrates.
source: Uroderma bilobatum support flight with some of the fastest metabolic incorporation rates and dynamic circulating cortisol in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by cortisol measurements showing 10-15 fold increases from baseline to restraint-induced values.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum will exchange fat reserves within 24 hr.
source: These bats will exchange fat reserves within 24 hr, meaning that they must survive on the food of the day and are at daily risk of starvation.
evidence: This is supported by stable isotope turnover experiments showing t50 for fat replacement after 13 hr.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum must survive on the food of the day and are at daily risk of starvation.
source: These bats will exchange fat reserves within 24 hr, meaning that they must survive on the food of the day and are at daily risk of starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid fat turnover data showing 24 hr exchange of reserves.

claim: Energy intake, incorporation and expenditure are fundamental to animal behavior and evolution.
source: Energy intake, incorporation and expenditure are fundamental to animal behavior and evolution (Brown et al., 2004; Weiner, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Animals must balance between generating enough metabolic power to find and acquire food and maintaining sufficient reserves to sustain daily maintenance, repair and reproduction.
source: Animals must balance between generating enough metabolic power to find and acquire food and maintaining sufficient reserves to sustain daily maintenance, and repair and reproduce.
evidence: This is a general principle of animal energetics based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Energy balance requirements can drive the foraging strategies of entire clades.
source: This basic requirement of life can drive the foraging strategies of entire clades (Williams et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2014.

claim: Extensive links among various behavioral and physiological strategies have evolved in response to single ecological pressures including diet and pathogen environments.
source: extensive links among various behavioral and physiological strategies have evolved in response to single ecological pressures including diet and pathogen environments (Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2012.

claim: Energy expenditure is additive across parallel aspects of physiology.
source: This is largely a consequence of the sequential and linear process of energetic input (feeding), and that energy expenditure is additive across parallel aspects of physiology (Weiner, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weiner, 1992.

claim: Data collected in laboratory settings may not reflect the full range of strategies animals employ to deal with energetic dilemmas.
source: Furthermore, accumulating evidence shows that data collected in laboratory settings may not reflect the full range of strategies animals employ to deal with this energetic dilemma (Bishop et al., 2015; Bowlin et al., 2005; Calisi and Bentley, 2009; Geiser et al., 2007; Ward et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing differences between lab and field measurements.

claim: Flight is one of the most efficient modes of locomotion per unit distance traveled.
source: While flight is one of the most efficient modes of locomotion per unit distance traveled, it is costlier per unit time than any other mode of locomotion (Norberg, 1990; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Norberg, 1990 and Schmidt-Nielsen, 1979.

claim: Flight is costlier per unit time than any other mode of locomotion.
source: While flight is one of the most efficient modes of locomotion per unit distance traveled, it is costlier per unit time than any other mode of locomotion (Norberg, 1990; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Norberg, 1990 and Schmidt-Nielsen, 1979.

claim: Both birds and bats have undergone dramatic physiological reorganization that emphasizes the need to supply fuel to large flight muscles.
source: To fulfill the exceptional demands of powered flight, both birds and bats have undergone dramatic physiological reorganization that emphasizes the need to supply fuel to large flight muscles (Maina, 2000; Norberg, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maina, 2000 and Norberg, 1990.

claim: Hearts and lungs of bats are larger than those of non-flying mammals of comparable size.
source: In comparison to those of non-flying mammals of comparable size, hearts and lungs of bats are larger and have higher blood oxygen transport potential, delivering more oxygen per heart beat than non-flying terrestrial mammals (Neuweiler, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neuweiler, 2000.

claim: Bats have higher blood oxygen transport potential than non-flying terrestrial mammals.
source: In comparison to those of non-flying mammals of comparable size, hearts and lungs of bats are larger and have higher blood oxygen transport potential, delivering more oxygen per heart beat than non-flying terrestrial mammals (Neuweiler, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neuweiler, 2000.

claim: Bats deliver more oxygen per heart beat than non-flying terrestrial mammals.
source: In comparison to those of non-flying mammals of comparable size, hearts and lungs of bats are larger and have higher blood oxygen transport potential, delivering more oxygen per heart beat than non-flying terrestrial mammals (Neuweiler, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neuweiler, 2000.

claim: Bats use some of the highest mass-specific metabolic rates during flight, 3–5 times greater than any other mammals.
source: Bats use some of the highest mass-specific metabolic rates during flight; 3–5 times greater than any other mammals and maximum increases of 15–16 times minimum resting metabolic rates (Speakman and Thomas, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Speakman and Thomas, 2003.

claim: Bats show maximum increases of 15–16 times minimum resting metabolic rates during flight.
source: Bats use some of the highest mass-specific metabolic rates during flight; 3–5 times greater than any other mammals and maximum increases of 15–16 times minimum resting metabolic rates (Speakman and Thomas, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Speakman and Thomas, 2003.

claim: Bats launch themselves directly into energy-demanding flight at the onset of their activity period on an empty stomach.
source: Bats launch themselves directly into energy-demanding flight at the onset of their activity period and on an empty stomach, fueling flight by limited fat reserves (Voigt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2010.

claim: Bats fuel initial flight by limited fat reserves.
source: Bats launch themselves directly into energy-demanding flight at the onset of their activity period and on an empty stomach, fueling flight by limited fat reserves (Voigt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2010.

claim: Some bats reduce metabolic rates by 99% during torpor when ambient temperatures are lower than their thermoneutral zone.
source: By entering a distinct low-energy state characterized by low body temperature, some bats reduce metabolic rates by 99% during torpor when ambient temperatures are lower than their thermoneutral zone (Geiser and Stawski, 2011; Ruf and Geiser, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geiser and Stawski, 2011 and Ruf and Geiser, 2015.

claim: In tropical and sub-tropical regions where ambient temperatures are high, it may be impossible to lower body temperature beyond critical minimum temperatures to save energy.
source: In tropical and sub-tropical regions where ambient temperatures are high, it may be impossible to lower body temperature beyond these critical minimum temperatures to save energy, therefore reductions in heart rate may reflect reductions in cellular respiration rates and gene expression in multiple pathways and be an effective measure of energetic conservation (Dechmann et al., 2011; Dzal et al., 2015; McNab, 1969; Storey and Storey, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents inference about tropical bat physiology.

claim: Reductions in heart rate may reflect reductions in cellular respiration rates and gene expression in multiple pathways.
source: In tropical and sub-tropical regions where ambient temperatures are high, it may be impossible to lower body temperature beyond these critical minimum temperatures to save energy, therefore reductions in heart rate may reflect reductions in cellular respiration rates and gene expression in multiple pathways and be an effective measure of energetic conservation (Dechmann et al., 2011; Dzal et al., 2015; McNab, 1969; Storey and Storey, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dechmann et al., 2011; Dzal et al., 2015; McNab, 1969; Storey and Storey, 2004.

claim: Heart rate has a quadratic relationship with metabolic oxygen consumption.
source: Heart rate has a quadratic relationship with metabolic oxygen consumption (Bishop and Spivey, 2013; Grubb, 1982)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bishop and Spivey, 2013 and Grubb, 1982.

claim: Heart rates in bats may more than double in the transition from rest to flight.
source: Heart rates in bats may more than double in the transition from rest to flight, reflecting enormous flight power requirements (Thomas, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas, 1975.

claim: In a tropical insectivorous bat, heart rate increases from 129 bpm in the roost to 847 bpm during flight, a six-fold increase.
source: In a tropical insectivorous bat, heart rate increases from 129 bpm in the roost to 847 bpm during flight, a six-fold increase that is larger than predicted from other captive bats in wind tunnels (Dechmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dechmann et al., 2011.

claim: Bar-headed geese traverse the Himalayas with heart rates of 250–475 bpm, 20% lower than expected from captive measures.
source: For example, bar-headed geese traverse the Himalayas with heart rates of 250–475 bpm (Bishop et al., 2015), 20% lower than what is expected from captive measures (Ward et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bishop et al., 2015 and Ward et al., 2002.

claim: During migration, heart rates in Swainson's thrushes are 10% lower than comparable long flights in wind tunnels.
source: during migration, heart rates in Swainson's thrushes are 10% lower than comparable long flights in wind tunnels (Bowlin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bowlin et al., 2005.

claim: Bats fuel their enormous demand for power by directly and rapidly metabolizing ingested food.
source: Once they begin to feed, bats fuel their enormous demand for power by directly and rapidly metabolizing ingested food, but this can lead to high risk of starvation via rapid fat turnover (Caviedes-Vidal et al., 2008; Voigt and Speakman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caviedes-Vidal et al., 2008 and Voigt and Speakman, 2007.

claim: Rapid metabolism of ingested food can lead to high risk of starvation via rapid fat turnover in bats.
source: Once they begin to feed, bats fuel their enormous demand for power by directly and rapidly metabolizing ingested food, but this can lead to high risk of starvation via rapid fat turnover (Caviedes-Vidal et al., 2008; Voigt and Speakman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caviedes-Vidal et al., 2008 and Voigt and Speakman, 2007.

claim: Glucocorticoids are key integrators between the environment and energy balance that ensure rapid response to changes in energetic needs.
source: One mechanism that may help animals to adjust the timing and intensity of shifts in metabolic scopes are glucocorticoids. They are key integrators between the environment and energy balance that ensure rapid response to changes in energetic needs (Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2012.

claim: Elevated levels of glucocorticoid hormones in blood plasma suppress glycogen formation and promote gluconeogenesis.
source: Elevated levels of glucocorticoid hormones in blood plasma suppress glycogen formation and promote gluconeogenesis (Haase et al., 2016), fat oxidation (Brillon et al., 1995), and play a primary role in energy balance (Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haase et al., 2016.

claim: Elevated levels of glucocorticoid hormones promote fat oxidation.
source: Elevated levels of glucocorticoid hormones in blood plasma suppress glycogen formation and promote gluconeogenesis (Haase et al., 2016), fat oxidation (Brillon et al., 1995), and play a primary role in energy balance (Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brillon et al., 1995.

claim: Glucocorticoids play a primary role in energy balance.
source: Elevated levels of glucocorticoid hormones in blood plasma suppress glycogen formation and promote gluconeogenesis (Haase et al., 2016), fat oxidation (Brillon et al., 1995), and play a primary role in energy balance (Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008.

claim: Most bats that have been studied show high baseline glucocorticoid concentrations.
source: Most bats that have been studied show high baseline glucocorticoid concentrations (Reeder et al., 2004; 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reeder et al., 2004 and 2006.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum are central-place foragers that leave a stable roost location to feed primarily on juice extracted from ripe figs (Ficus spp).
source: To better understand the interplay of energy expenditure and conservation, we describe the daily energetic life of Peters' tent-making bat (Uroderma bilobatum, family Phyllostomidae) in Gamboa, Panamá. These bats are central-place foragers that leave a stable roost location to feed primarily on juice extracted from ripe figs (Ficus spp).
evidence: This is a description of the study species' natural history based on observation.

claim: Four bats were tracked for heart rates for 13.6 ± 4.9 hr each day for two to four days (13 days total).
source: We tracked the heart rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) of four bats for 13.6 ± 4.9 hr (mean ± SD) each day for two to four days (13 days total).
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol and sample size.

claim: Tracking included 4.03 ± 0.05 hr of activity outside of the roost at night and approximately 12 hr in the roost during the day for 350 hr of total recording time.
source: This included 4.03 ± 0.05 hr of activity outside of the roost at night and the approximately 12 hr that bats spend in their roost during the day for 350 hr of total recording time.
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol and total observation time.

claim: All bats left their roosts between 18:00 – 18:30.
source: All bats left their roosts between 18:00 – 18:30 and flew three to seven minutes to their initial foraging sites.
evidence: This is based on direct observation during radio tracking.

claim: Bats flew three to seven minutes to their initial foraging sites.
source: All bats left their roosts between 18:00 – 18:30 and flew three to seven minutes to their initial foraging sites.
evidence: This is based on direct observation during radio tracking.

claim: Bats executed multiple short flights of 1–2 min each (mean ± SD: 1 ± 1.5 min).
source: Bats executed multiple short flights of 1–2 min each (mean ± SD: 1 ± 1.5 min) that were consistent with flying to a fruiting tree, selecting a fruit, and carrying it to a separate feeding perch.
evidence: This is based on direct observation during radio tracking.

claim: Flight accounted for 13 ± 6% (30.6 ± 15.6 min) of the time outside of the roost.
source: During our tracking, flight accounted for 13 ± 6% (30.6 ± 15.6 min) of the time outside of the roost.
evidence: This is calculated from radio tracking observations.

claim: All food trees located during tracking were Ficus insipida.
source: We were able to locate several food trees, all of which were Ficus insipida, but all bats also fed for short periods across the Panama Canal at sites inaccessible during tracking.
evidence: This is based on direct observation during radio tracking.

claim: Bats returned to their day roosts between 22:30 – 06:00.
source: Bats returned to their day roosts between 22:30 – 06:00.
evidence: This is based on direct observation during radio tracking.

claim: All bats returned to their home roost each night where they remained for the rest of the day.
source: All bats returned to their home roost each night where they remained for the rest of the day.
evidence: This is based on direct observation during radio tracking.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum used a large range in heart rates across the day, ranging from 173 to 1066 bpm.
source: Uroderma bilobatum used a large range in heart rates (fH) across the day, ranging from 173 to 1066 bpm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly measured from heart rate telemetry data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bats expend 4.9 ± 0.8 kJ h−1 during flight (mean ± SD; fH: 766 ± 56 bpm).
source: Analysis of activity-specific fH shows that bats expend 4.9 ± 0.8 kJ h−1 during flight (mean ± SD; fH: 766 ± 56 bpm, Figure 1).
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Minimum fH of flying bats was 750 bpm.
source: Amplitude fluctuations of the fH radio signals show that minimum fH of flying bats was 750 bpm.
evidence: This is determined from analysis of radio signal amplitude fluctuations.

claim: Maximum recorded flying fH was 1066 bpm.
source: Maximum recorded flying fH was 1066 bpm.
evidence: This is directly measured from heart rate telemetry data.

claim: Uroderma bilobatum needed to generate a minimum of 0.98 W to fly (3.5 kJ h−1).
source: Uroderma bilobatum then needed to generate a minimum of 0.98 W to fly (3.5 kJ h−1), but flight typically had higher costs of 1.36 ± 0.23 W with a maximum recorded output of 2.3 W.
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data using the calibration equation.

claim: Flight typically had costs of 1.36 ± 0.23 W with a maximum recorded output of 2.3 W.
source: Uroderma bilobatum then needed to generate a minimum of 0.98 W to fly (3.5 kJ h−1), but flight typically had higher costs of 1.36 ± 0.23 W with a maximum recorded output of 2.3 W.
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data using the calibration equation.

claim: Mass-specific metabolic power during flight was 75.89 ± 11.9 W kg−1 with a maximum of 145.6 W kg−1.
source: This is a mass-specific metabolic power of 75.89 ± 11.9 W kg−1 and a maximum mass specific power of 145.6 W kg−1.
evidence: This is calculated from the power output and body mass data.

claim: Nightly non-flight activity when bats were stationary required 2.2 ± 1.1 kJ h−1 (fH: 492 ± 128 bpm).
source: Nightly non-flight activity when bats were stationary required 2.2 ± 1.1 kJ h−1 (fH: 492 ± 128 bpm, Figure 1).
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: U. bilobatum periodically lower fH to 200–250 bpm from a mean fH of 374 ± 112 bpm throughout their daily resting periods.
source: Surprisingly, U. bilobatum periodically lower fH to 200–250 bpm from a mean fH of 374 ± 112 bpm throughout their daily resting periods where they remain relatively inactive in their roosts, and during which they consume 1.2 ± 0.8 kJ h−1 (0.33 — 0.23 W or 18.84 ± 13.59 W kg−1, Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly measured from heart rate telemetry data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: During daily resting periods, bats consume 1.2 ± 0.8 kJ h−1 (0.33 — 0.23 W or 18.84 ± 13.59 W kg−1).
source: Surprisingly, U. bilobatum periodically lower fH to 200–250 bpm from a mean fH of 374 ± 112 bpm throughout their daily resting periods where they remain relatively inactive in their roosts, and during which they consume 1.2 ± 0.8 kJ h−1 (0.33 — 0.23 W or 18.84 ± 13.59 W kg−1, Figure 2).
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bats suppress fH by 30% 2–3 times per hour (mean: 1.54 ± 1.18 sd times per hour) for 5–7 min throughout the day.
source: Bats suppress fH by 30% 2–3 times per hour (mean: 1.54 ± 1.18 sd times per hour) for 5–7 min throughout the day (Figure 2).
evidence: This is calculated from analysis of heart rate telemetry data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: This cyclic bradycardia is a yet undescribed strategy that was only detectable through complete sampling of daily heart rate recordings.
source: This cyclic bradycardia is a yet undescribed strategy that was only detectable through complete sampling of daily heart rate recordings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the novelty of the finding and the methodology used.

claim: All bats employed these reduced heart rates but one individual only used them on two of the four days it was observed.
source: All bats employed these reduced heart rates but one individual only used them on two of the four days it was observed.
evidence: This is based on analysis of individual heart rate patterns across observation days.

claim: Lowered heart rate resulted in a median resting metabolic rate (RMR) of 0.54 ± 0.01 kJ h−1 compared to RMR 0.75 ± 0.04 kJ h−1 at higher mean fH.
source: This lowered heart rate resulted in a median resting metabolic rate (RMR) of 0.54 ± 0.01 kJ h−1 compared to RMR 0.75 ± 0.04 kJ h−1 at higher mean fH.
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data using the calibration equation.

claim: Typical field metabolic rate (FMR) is 45.79 kJ if a bat spends 2 hr in flight and executes daily cyclic bradycardia.
source: Using the mean energetic expenditure by each bat on each night it was tracked (Supplementary file 1) we can estimate typical field metabolic rate (FMR) of 45.79 kJ if a bat spends 2 hr in flight and executes daily cyclic bradycardia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data and activity budgets, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mean metabolic scope was 5.39 ± 1.80 based on median values for each individual.
source: Based on median values for each individual mean metabolic scope was 5.39 ± 1.80.
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of maximum to minimum metabolic rates.

claim: Cyclic bradycardia saved U. bilobatum 0.3–0.5 kJ h−1 or 3.5–6 kJ total over the 12 hr resting phase which is 10% (7.6–13.1%) of their total FMR.
source: This short, cyclic bradycardia then saved U. bilobatum 0.3–0.5 kJ h−1 or 3.5–6 kJ total over the 12 hr resting phase which is 10% (7.6–13.1%) of their total FMR.
evidence: This is calculated from the difference in energy expenditure with and without bradycardia.

claim: RMR derived from median heart rates of resting bats in their natural roosts during the day is 0.54 kJ h−1 or 0.27 W, estimating a RMR of 13.0 kJ day−1.
source: Using the energetic expenditure derived from median heart rates of resting bats in their natural roosts during the day (0.54 kJ h−1 or 0.27 W) we can estimate a RMR of 13.0 kJ day−1, which closely approximates previous measures of BMR (12.8 kJ day−1 [McNab, 1969]).
evidence: This is calculated from heart rate data and compared to literature values.

claim: This RMR closely approximates previous measures of BMR (12.8 kJ day−1).
source: Using the energetic expenditure derived from median heart rates of resting bats in their natural roosts during the day (0.54 kJ h−1 or 0.27 W) we can estimate a RMR of 13.0 kJ day−1, which closely approximates previous measures of BMR (12.8 kJ day−1 [McNab, 1969]).
evidence: This compares the calculated RMR to a cited BMR value from McNab, 1969.

claim: Estimated FMR is ca. 46 kJ day−1, which is within the general predictions for FMR based on body mass from a broad taxonomic sampling of studies using doubly-labeled water.
source: The subsequently low heart rates and activity patterns estimate an estimated FMR of ca. 46 kJ day−1 (Bishop and Spivey, 2013), which is within the general predictions for FMR based on body mass from a broad taxonomic sampling of studies using doubly-labeled water (Speakman, 2005).
evidence: This compares the calculated FMR to predictions from Speakman, 2005.

claim: The cyclic bradycardia during daytime rest is unprecedented.
source: The cyclic bradycardia during daytime rest in our study is unprecedented.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to existing literature.

claim: When humans and cats sleep their heart rate slows immediately prior to the elevation of heart rates during REM cycles.
source: It is possible that these cycles are linked to REM and pre-REM sleep, but when humans and cats sleep their heart rate slows immediately prior to the elevation of heart rates during REM cycles (Taylor et al., 1985; Verrier et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 1985 and Verrier et al., 1998.

claim: In humans and cats, the change in heart rate during sleep lasts only seconds and amounts to a total change of 3–5% from the resting heart rate.
source: In both taxa the change in heart rate lasts only seconds and amounts to a total change of 3–5% from the resting heart rate as compared to the minutes-long 30% reduction in U. bilboatum.
evidence: This is inferred from the citations about human and cat sleep patterns and compared to the bat data.

claim: Hibernating ground squirrels show irregular heart rates that speed up for 30–50 s before slowing again to a steady rate.
source: A reversed pattern in heart rate is found in hibernating ground squirrels that show irregular heart rates that speed up for 30–50 s before slowing again to a steady rate (Milsom et al., 1993; Milsom et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Milsom et al., 1993 and 1999.

claim: Bradycardia is common aspect of the dive response where diving mammals slow their heart rates to conserve oxygen when submerged for long periods.
source: Bradycardia is common aspect of the dive response where diving mammals slow their heart rates to conserve oxygen when submerged for long periods (Noren et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noren et al., 2012.

claim: Mammals in torpor are bradycardic.
source: Mammals in torpor are also bradycardic (Currie et al., 2014; Dechmann et al., 2011; Elvert and Heldmaier, 2005; Heldmaier et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Animals enter torpor and hibernation through controlled reductions of heart rate via increased inter-beat interval and skipped beats.
source: Animals enter torpor and hibernation through controlled reductions of heart rate via increased inter-beat interval and skipped beats (Elvert and Heldmaier, 2005; Milsom et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elvert and Heldmaier, 2005 and Milsom et al., 1999.

claim: Bats and hummingbirds in torpor and at rest have showed low and constant heart rates without any indication of the cycling observed in U. bilobatum.
source: Thus far, bats and hummingbirds in torpor and at rest have showed low and constant heart rates without any indication of the cycling we observe (Currie et al., 2014; Dechmann et al., 2011; Schaub and Prinzinger, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Currie et al., 2014; Dechmann et al., 2011; Schaub and Prinzinger, 1999.

claim: Species that are capable of daily torpor generally lower their body temperatures to maximize energetic savings, particularly when exposed to cold temperatures.
source: Species that are capable of daily torpor generally lower their body temperatures to maximize energetic savings, particularly when exposed to cold temperatures (Ruf and Geiser, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruf and Geiser, 2015.

claim: Torpor commonly occurs in tropical and sub-tropical mammals at temperatures below 24°C.
source: Species that are capable of daily torpor generally lower their body temperatures to maximize energetic savings, particularly when exposed to cold temperatures (Ruf and Geiser, 2015), and this commonly occurs in tropical and sub-tropical mammals at temperatures below 24°C (Canale et al., 2012; Geiser and Stawski, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canale et al., 2012 and Geiser and Stawski, 2011.

claim: U. bilobatum actively defend their body temperatures when exposed to cold, and more than triple metabolic rates to maintain a body temperature of 36°C at ambient temperatures of 10°C vs 30°C.
source: However, a similar torpor response is not possible for the tropical U. bilobatum. Instead, they actively defend their body temperatures when exposed to cold, and more than triple metabolic rates to maintain a body temperature of 36°C at ambient temperatures of 10°C vs 30°C (McNab, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McNab, 1969.

claim: In respirometry calibrations, U. bilobatum maintained a constant body temperature around 37°C across the measured range of heart rates of 300–800 bpm.
source: In our respirometry calibrations, U. bilobatum maintained a constant body temperature around 37°C across the measured range of heart rates of 300–800 bpm.
evidence: This is based on data from respirometry experiments.

claim: Bats may alter heart rate dynamics independently of body temperature.
source: In fact, they may alter heart rate dynamics independently of body temperature (Tøien et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tøien et al., 2011.

claim: The low heart rates observed are similar to the minimum resting heart rates of small bats (i.e., 200–400 bpm) in thermoneutral conditions.
source: The low heart rates we observed are similar to the minimum resting heart rates of small bats (i.e., 200–400 bpm) in thermonetural conditions (Currie et al., 2015; Kulzer, 1967; Leitner, 1966; Leitner and Nelson, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Currie et al., 2015; Kulzer, 1967; Leitner, 1966; Leitner and Nelson, 1967.

claim: The thermoneutral zone for U. bilobatum is reported to be 29–35°C.
source: The thermoneutral zone for U. bilobatum is reported to be 29–35°C (McNab, 1969; Rodríguez-Herrera et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to McNab, 1969 and Rodríguez-Herrera et al., 2016.

claim: The field site ambient temperature (mean: 25.87 ± 1.21°C, range: 23.38–28.24°C) is slightly lower than the thermoneutral zone for U. bilobatum.
source: The thermoneutral zone for U. bilobatum is reported to be 29–35°C (McNab, 1969; Rodríguez-Herrera et al., 2016), which is still slightly higher than the ambient temperature of our field site (mean: 25.87 ± 1.21°C, range: 23.38–28.24°C.
evidence: This compares measured ambient temperature to the cited thermoneutral zone.

claim: There are relatively few data on the heart rates of free-flying animals.
source: There are relatively few data on the heart rates of free-flying animals (Green, 2011) all of which are larger than U. bilobatum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Green, 2011.

claim: The heart rate derived estimate for cost of flight in U. bilobatum (1.36 ± 0.23 W, range 0.98–2.3 W) was slightly lower than mass loss estimates for bats of similar sizes and wing shapes (1.96–2.45 W).
source: The heart rate derived estimate for cost of flight in U. bilobatum (1.36 ± 0.23 W, range 0.98–2.3 W) was slightly lower than mass loss estimates for bats of similar sizes and wing shapes (1.96–2.45 W: (von Busse et al., 2013; Winter and von Helversen, 1998).
evidence: This compares the calculated flight costs to literature values from von Busse et al., 2013 and Winter and von Helversen, 1998.

claim: U. bilobatum show a mass specific power of 76 W kg−1 with a maximum output of 145 W kg−1, which is within the power requirements of bats that are up to 44 times larger.
source: However, U. bilobatum show a mass specific power of 76 W kg−1 with a maximum output of 145 W kg−1, which is within the power requirements of bats that are up to 44 times larger (Carpenter, 1986; Thomas, 1975).
evidence: This compares the calculated mass-specific power to literature values from Carpenter, 1986 and Thomas, 1975.

claim: The ability to rapidly fuel metabolism through ingested food seems to be a common adaptation among hummingbirds and bats with diets of simple carbohydrates and the fastest incorporation rates measured for vertebrates.
source: The ability to rapidly fuel metabolism through ingested food seems to be a common adaptation among hummingbirds and bats with diets of simple carbohydrates and the fastest incorporation rates measured for vertebrates (Welch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Welch et al., 2016.

claim: Nectarivorous hummingbirds (3–5 g) and bats (10 g) fuel 50% of their metabolism within 3–9 min of feeding.
source: Nectarivorous hummingbirds (3–5 g) and bats (10 g) fuel 50% of their metabolism within 3–9 min of feeding (Suarez et al., 2011; Voigt and Speakman, 2007; Welch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suarez et al., 2011; Voigt and Speakman, 2007; Welch et al., 2008.

claim: Other fruit-eating bats use incorporation rates of 10–12 min regardless of body size.
source: In contrast, other fruit-eating bats use incorporation rates of 10–12 min regardless of body size (Amitai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amitai et al., 2010.

claim: Rapid incorporation is mediated through paracellular absorption.
source: These comparative data indicate strong pressure on all flying frugivores, regardless of size, to mobilize ingested food to power flight and this is mediated through paracellular absorption (Caviedes-Vidal et al., 2008; Price et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caviedes-Vidal et al., 2008 and Price et al., 2014.

claim: Frugivorous bats deplete the large glycogen stores in their liver within 24 hr.
source: Frugivorous bats deplete the large glycogen stores in their liver within 24 hr (Pinheiro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pinheiro et al., 2006.

claim: Basal glucocorticoid values of other bat species are especially high for mammals of their size (100–800 ng ml−1).
source: Basal glucocorticoid values of other bat species are especially high for mammals of their size (100–800 ng ml−1; (Reeder et al., 2004; 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reeder et al., 2004 and 2006.

claim: Other bat species show large potential maximal output when challenged with ACTH.
source: Basal glucocorticoid values of other bat species are especially high for mammals of their size (100–800 ng ml−1; (Reeder et al., 2004; 2006) and show large potential maximal output when challenged with ACTH (Lewanzik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewanzik et al., 2012.

claim: The difference between baseline and restraint-induced circulating cortisol in female U. bilobatum is similar to the extremes found in lemmings (Lemmus trimucronatus) that seasonally elevate their baseline corticosterone values by 10–80 times to concentrations of over 4000 ng ml−1.
source: However, the difference between baseline and restraint-induced circulating cortisol especially in female U. bilobatum is more similar to the extremes found in lemmings (Lemmus trimucronatus) that seasonally elevate their baseline corticosterone values by 10–80 times to concentrations of over 4000 ng ml−1 (Romero et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Romero et al., 2008.

claim: Flying squirrels (Glaucomys sp) elevate cortisol values 38–40% above already high baseline values.
source: or in flying squirrels (Glaucomys sp) that elevate cortisol values 38–40% above already high baseline values (Desantis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Desantis et al., 2016.

claim: The low baseline cortisol values may be a consequence of capturing resting or sleeping animals in their day roosts at least 4 hr after sunrise when circulating glucocorticoids were at their lowest.
source: The low baselines we found may be a consequence of capturing resting or sleeping animals in their day roosts at least 4 hr after sunrise when circulating glucocorticoids were at their lowest (Sapolsky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is speculation about the timing of sampling supported by citation to Sapolsky et al., 2000.

claim: By suppressing glucocorticoid secretion during rest these bats are able to further minimize energetic expenditure and lower their metabolic rates.
source: We suggest that rapid increases in circulating cortisol levels during the acute stress response act in concert to mobilize energy stores, but more importantly, by suppressing glucocorticoid secretion during rest these bats are able to further minimize energetic expenditure and lower their metabolic rates (Haase et al., 2016; Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008; Palme et al., 2005)
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Haase et al., 2016; Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008; Palme et al., 2005.

claim: Suppressing glucocorticoid secretion during rest minimizes additional fat oxidation.
source: by suppressing glucocorticoid secretion during rest these bats are able to further minimize energetic expenditure and lower their metabolic rates (Haase et al., 2016; Nieuwenhuizen and Rutters, 2008; Palme et al., 2005) and minimize additional fat oxidation (Brillon et al., 1995).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Brillon et al., 1995.

claim: Some bats, including U. bilobatum take advantage of their roosts to leverage social information and identify newly available food items.
source: Unpredictable fruit availability can have dramatic effects on survival and some bats, including U. bilobatum take advantage of their roosts to leverage social information and identify newly available food items (O'Mara et al., 2014a; Ramakers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Mara et al., 2014a and Ramakers et al., 2016.

claim: Four adult Uroderma bilobatum (2f/2m, 18.1 ± 1.5 g body mass) were captured from their day roosts in Gamboa, Panamá in December 2014.
source: We captured 4 adult Uroderma bilobatum (2f/2m, 18.1 ± 1.5 g body mass) from their day roosts in Gamboa, Panamá in December 2014.
evidence: This describes the study subjects and capture details.

claim: Heart rate transmitters added 4.5 ± 0.04% of body mass.
source: This added 4.5 ± 0.04% of body mass and is within the range of the additional loading (5%) that should have minimal impact on behavior and physiology of bats and birds (Aldridge and Brigham, 1988; Barron et al., 2010; Elliott, 2016; O'Mara et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is a measurement of transmitter mass relative to body mass, with citations supporting minimal impact.

claim: After calibration, animals were tracked for 2–6 days (mean: 3.75 d).
source: After calibration of heart rate versus oxygen consumption (below) animals were tracked for 2–6 days (mean: 3.75 d).
evidence: This describes the tracking duration.

claim: Three of the four bats were recaptured and had their transmitters removed.
source: We recaptured three of the four bats and removed their transmitters.
evidence: This describes the recapture success.

claim: Bats lost 0.0–0.5 g (0.17 ± 0.29 g) which is within the daily mass fluctuations (1–2 g) observed in this species.
source: Bats lost 0.0–0.5 g (0.17 ± 0.29 g) which is within the daily mass fluctuations (1–2 g) observed in this species (O'Mara, unpublished data).
evidence: This is a measurement of mass change compared to typical fluctuations.

claim: Bats remained normothermic throughout the respirometry experiment with Tb = 36.9 ± 1.6°C.
source: Bats remained normothermic throughout the experiment with Tb = 36.9 ± 1.6°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured body temperature data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Heart rate provided a better fit in a single factor generalized linear mixed effect model of energy consumption than body temperature (R2adjusted = 0.758 vs R2adjusted = 0.145, respectively).
source: Heart rate provided a better fit in a single factor generalized linear mixed effect model (bat identity as a random effect) of energy consumption than body temperature (R2adjusted = 0.758 vs R2adjusted = 0.145, respectively)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of model fits.

claim: The inclusion of Tb in a two-factor model did not improve the model's predictive ability.
source: and the inclusion of Tb in a two-factor model did not improve the model's predictive ability.
evidence: This is a result from statistical model comparison.

claim: In the best-fit model, energy expenditure was related to fH as (kJ h−1)=0.004 * fh - 0.3228.
source: In the best-fit model, energy expenditure was related to fH as (kJ h−1)=0.004 * fh - 0.3228 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is the calibration equation derived from respirometry data, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Heart rate of free-ranging bats was recorded during 2–6 days and nights using telemetry receivers connected to 3-element Yagi antennae.
source: We recorded fH of the four free-ranging bats during 2–6 days and nights using telemetry receivers (AR8000, AOR Ltd) connected to 3-element Yagi antennae (Sparrow Systems).
evidence: This describes the telemetry methodology.

claim: Transmitter signal could be detected within 70–100 meters in the forest and up to a kilometer over open space.
source: Transmitter signal could be detected within 70–100 meters in the forest and up to a kilometer over open space (the Panama Canal).
evidence: This describes the detection range of the telemetry system.

claim: This gave 18–20 hr of heart rate recordings per individual per day for a total of 350 hr.
source: This gave us 18–20 hr of heart rate recordings per individual per day for a total of 350 hr.
evidence: This describes the total recording time.

claim: Daytime mean ambient temperature was 25.87 ± 1.21°C (mean daytime minimum to mean maximum: 23.38–28.24).
source: Daytime mean ambient temperature was 25.87 ± 1.21°C (mean daytime minimum to mean maximum: 23.38–28.24), and mean nightly ambient temperature was 23.74 ± 0.50°C (mean nightly minimum to mean maximum: 22.74–24.78°C).
evidence: This is ambient temperature data from the field site.

claim: Mean nightly ambient temperature was 23.74 ± 0.50°C (mean nightly minimum to mean maximum: 22.74–24.78°C).
source: Daytime mean ambient temperature was 25.87 ± 1.21°C (mean daytime minimum to mean maximum: 23.38–28.24), and mean nightly ambient temperature was 23.74 ± 0.50°C (mean nightly minimum to mean maximum: 22.74–24.78°C).
evidence: This is ambient temperature data from the field site.

claim: After the initial sample collection, bats were fed either freshly-collected Ficus insipida, or approximately 1.5 ml of a solution of 20% (w/w) agave nectar, 2% (w/w) Nutri-Cal and water.
source: After the initial sample collection (time 0), bats were removed from the container and fed either freshly-collected Ficus insipida, or approximately 1.5 ml of a solution of 20% (w/w) agave nectar (Organic Blue Agave Nectar, Wholesome Sweeteners, Sugar Land Texas, USA), 2% (w/w) Nutri-Cal (Vétoquinol Prolab Inc, Princeville, Québec, Canada) and water using a transfer pipette.
evidence: This describes the experimental diet composition.

claim: Breath samples were collected at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, and 90 min after the initial feeding.
source: Breath samples were collected at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, and 90 min after the initial feeding.
evidence: This describes the sampling protocol.

claim: Bats' exhaled breath was rapidly enriched in 13C and reached an asymptotic value of −16.5 ± 2.0 ‰ 50 min after initial feeding.
source: Their exhaled breath was rapidly enriched in 13C and reached an asymptotic value of −16.5 ± 2.0 ‰ 50 min after initial feeding (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is measured from stable isotope analysis of breath samples, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The asymptotic δ13C value is lower than the δ13C value of the diet (δ13Cdiet = −12.0 ± 0.1 ‰, t = −12.6, df = 32, p<0.001).
source: which is lower than the δ13C value of the diet and indicates that fat or glycogen stores continued to be metabolized (δ13Cdiet = −12.0 ± 0.1 ‰, t = −12.6, df = 32, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of breath and diet isotope values.

claim: Overall δ13C breath enrichment followed a mean single pool incorporation model of δ13C breath(t)=−16.575–12.841e-0.081t, with 50% of metabolism fueled by ingested food after only 8 min (t50 = 8.1 ± 15.6 min).
source: Overall δ13C breath enrichment followed a mean single pool incorporation model of δ13C breath(t)=−16.575–12.841e-0.081t, with 50% of metabolism fueled by ingested food after only 8 min (t50 = 8.1 ± 15.6 min).
evidence: This is a model fit to the isotope incorporation data.

claim: One distinctive bat (Individual A) showed a nearly linear enrichment curve with no asymptote.
source: The large standard deviation in t50 is due to one distinctive bat (Individual A) that showed a nearly linear enrichment curve with no asymptote (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes an outlier in the isotope incorporation data.

claim: If the outlier bat is excluded, t50 drops to 7.6 min and an incorporation curve of δ13C breath(t)=−16.497–13.138e-0.091t.
source: If this bat is excluded, t50 drops to 7.6 min and an incorporation curve of δ13C breath(t)=−16.497–13.138e-0.091t.
evidence: This is a recalculated model without the outlier.

claim: Bats fed with ripe Ficus indica (n = 6) did not show any change in δ13Cbreath over the course of the following 90 min (F1, 24 = 2.614, p=0.113).
source: Bats fed with ripe Ficus indica (n = 6) did not show any change in δ13Cbreath over the course of the following 90 min (Figure 4A, F1, 24 = 2.614, p=0.113).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control diet experiment, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Over three days, bats showed increasingly 13C enriched baseline δ13C breath values at the beginning of the night.
source: Over the course of the next three days, bats kept in captivity and fed on agave nectar showed increasingly 13C enriched baseline δ13C breath values at the beginning of the night (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is measured from stable isotope analysis over multiple days, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A mean single-pool exponential model of δ13Cbreath(t)=−16.412–12.901e-0.801t was estimated, with a t50 = 13.2 ± 4.6 hr.
source: We estimated a mean single-pool exponential model of δ13Cbreath(t)=−16.412–12.901e-0.801t, with a t50 = 13.2 ± 4.6 hr
evidence: This is a model fit to the multi-day isotope turnover data.

claim: By the third night bats approached an asymptotic starting value of −17.06 ± 1.27 ‰ which is not different from the asymptotic value of the initial feeding experiment (t13 = 0.91, p=0.38).
source: and by the third night bats approached an asymptotic starting value of −17.06 ± 1.27 ‰ which is not different from the asymptotic value of the initial feeding experiment (t13 = 0.91, p=0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of asymptotic values between experiments.

claim: Fifty percent of an individual's fat reserves are exchanged after 13–17 hr, and a carbon atom has a residency period of 1–2 days, with a full exchange of fat after 3 days.
source: This indicates that fifty percent of an individual's fat reserves are then exchanged after 13–17 hr, and a carbon atom has a residency period of 1–2 days, with a full exchange of fat after 3 days.
evidence: This is inferred from the isotope turnover model results.

claim: Bats captured at their roosts (15 F, 6 M) showed low baseline values of circulating cortisol concentrations that did not differ by sex (F: 64.81 ± 158.81 ng ml−1, M: 57.66 ± 137.07 ng ml−1, F1,19 = 0.009, p=0.92).
source: Bats captured at their roosts (15 F, 6 M) showed low baseline values of circulating cortisol concentrations (ng ml−1) that did not differ by sex (F: 64.81 ± 158.81 ng ml−1, M: 57.66 ± 137.07 ng ml−1, F1,19 = 0.009, p=0.92).
evidence: This is measured cortisol data with statistical comparison between sexes.

claim: When restrained in a cloth bag for one hour, bats showed restraint-induced values that were 10–15 times baseline conditions.
source: When restrained in a cloth bag for one hour they showed a strongly sex biased response: restraint-induced values were 10–15 times baseline conditions (Figure 5)
evidence: This is measured cortisol data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Restraint-induced cortisol values were two-fold greater in females than in males (F: 989.50 ± 450.78 ng ml−1, M: 428.34 ± 94.45 ng ml−1, F1,19 = 0.8.89, p=0.008).
source: and were two-fold greater in females than in males (F: 989.50 ± 450.78 ng ml−1, M: 428.34 ± 94.45 ng ml−1, F1,19 = 0.8.89, p=0.008).
evidence: This is measured cortisol data with statistical comparison between sexes.
